title: Acid Suppression and Esophageal Adenocarcinoma: A Critique of Causal Inference
content: This paper examines the inferential framework used to attribute the positive association between acid-suppressive therapy (AS) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) to confounding by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), a common indication for AS. The experimental literature has proposed several hypotheses by which AS may increase the risk of EAC, yet this possibility appears to have been discounted by observational studies that seek to isolate a GERD-independent component of the AS--EAC association and subsequently interpret their near-null estimates as evidence against causality. After presenting the causal hypotheses discussed in the in vivo literature, this paper argues that a patient's underlying reflux burden is a presupposed effect modifier under each of these hypothesized mechanisms, and that the findings of these observational studies do not distinguish confounding by GERD from any of these mechanisms. It concludes by discussing the broader epidemiological evidence base.
